newsitem.title: USA: US asks EU probe of airline reservations.
newsitem.headline: US asks EU probe of airline reservations.

text.p: The United States has formally asked the European Community to investigate whether a European airline reservation system is competing unfairly with U.S. counterparts, the Justice Department announced Monday.
The U.S. Justice Department asked EU competition authorities to investigate the "Amadeus" system, owned by Deutsche Lufthansa AG, Air France and Iberia Lineas Aereas de Espana SA.
The Justice Department said the request was made in January but kept secret until now to protect the integrity of the investigation.

"We believe there are indications that exclusionary conduct may be preventing U.S. companies from vigorously competing in computer reservation systems in Europe," Joel Klein, acting assistant attorney general in charge of the Antitrust Division, said in a statement.
The U.S. sent its preliminary findings to the Europeans after receiving complaints from Sabre Group Holdings Inc, a computer reservation system owned mostly by AMR Corp.

Sabre complained many airfares were not provided on a timely basis and some promotional and negotiated fares were never provided. Sabre said it was denied the ability to perform some ticketing functions, although Saber provided such functions to Amadeus.
The Justice Department said it was investigating similar allegedly anticompetitive conduct in some South American countries.

The request to the EU was the first formal request under a 1991 agreement for "positive comity," under which competition authorities in the United States and the European Community can seek to have each other look into potentially anticompetitive actions.
"The request demonstrates our commitment to cooperative antitrust enforcement with our European colleagues," said Klein.

The U.S. and EU have a more recent agreement spelling out in detailed form the conditions under which "positive comity" may be invoked. In a visit earlier this month, European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said he expected final approval of that agreement by the end of July.
